message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties**

| Property | Value / Description | Notes |
|----------|---------------------|-------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average) | Dominated by the most common isotope, ^1H. |
| **Isotopes** | ^1H (protium, 99.98 %), ^2H (deuterium, 0.02 %), ^3H (tritium, trace, radioactive) | Deuterium and tritium are used in nuclear fusion research. |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron; forms covalent bonds. |
| **Valence electrons** | 1 | Forms one covalent bond in most compounds. |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest among all elements. |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | Highest of all elements. |
| **Electron affinity** | –0.754 eV (–72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) | Negative, meaning H⁻ formation is endothermic. |
| **Molecular weight (H₂)** | 2.01588 g mol⁻¹ | |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) | Extremely low; remains gaseous at room temperature. |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | |
| **Density (at 0 °C, 1 atm)** | 0.08988 g cm⁻³ | Less dense than air; rises to ~0.09 g cm⁻³ at 25 °C. |
| **Specific heat capacity (gas)** | 14.304 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 25 °C) | High due to light mass. |
| **Molar volume (ideal gas)** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ (at 0 °C, 1 atm) | |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive; forms H₂O, acids, hydrides, etc. | Forms covalent bonds with many elements; reacts with halogens, metals, nonmetals. |
| **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; explosive mixture with air (4–75 % H₂). | Requires ignition source; used in rocket propellants. |
| **Acidity/Basicity** | Acts as a weak acid (forming H⁺) or base (forming H⁻) depending on context. | In aqueous solution, H⁺ is solvated as H₃O⁺. |
| **Bonding** | Typically forms single covalent bonds (H–H, H–X). | Can form diatomic molecules (H₂), hydrides (e.g., NaH), acids (e.g., HCl). |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series in UV/visible/IR. | Used in astrophysics to identify hydrogen in stars. |
| **Magnetic properties** | Diamagnetic (no unpaired electrons). | Weakly repelled by magnetic fields. |
| **Electrical conductivity** | Poor conductor as a gas; becomes metallic under extreme pressure (~400 GPa). | Metallic hydrogen is theorized to be a superconductor. |
| **Phase diagram** | Exhibits a solid, liquid, and gas phase; solid is a molecular crystal. | Under high pressure, transforms to metallic phases. |
| **Applications** | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells), rocket propellant, industrial hydrogenation, laboratory reagent, medical imaging (MRI contrast agents). | Also used in semiconductor manufacturing. |

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: Only one proton and one electron.
- **Highly reactive**: Forms a wide variety of compounds; essential in organic chemistry and industry.
- **Low boiling/melting points**: Remains gaseous at ordinary temperatures.
- **High ionization energy & electronegativity**: Makes it a strong oxidizing agent.
- **Flammable**: Requires careful handling; used in fuel cells and rockets.
- **Isotopic variants**: Deuterium and tritium have unique nuclear properties.

These properties make hydrogen a cornerstone of chemistry, physics, and emerging energy technologies.
